title: Predict string allocation and equality behavior and distinguish UTF-16 code units from user-perceived characters

rubric.point: Both `new string(...)` expressions create string objects; assigning `label` to `saved` only copies the reference.
`label += "!"` produces a new string and reassigns `label`; immutability leaves the object referenced by `saved` unchanged.
`saved == other` is true because string `==` compares content, and both contain `map`.
`ReferenceEquals(saved, other)` is false because the two constructor calls produced separate objects.

questions.model:
Each `new string(...)` creates a string object. `saved = label` copies the reference without creating another string.

`label += "!"` creates the string `"map!"` and assigns its reference to `label`. Strings are immutable, so the original object still contains `"map"`, and `saved` continues to reference it.

`saved == other` is `true`: both strings contain `"map"`. `object.ReferenceEquals(saved, other)` is `false`: their equal contents belong to separate objects created by the two constructor calls.

questions.prompt:
A C# string contains a rocket emoji followed by `n` with a combining tilde:

```csharp
string text = "\U0001F680n\u0303"; // 🚀ñ
```

Explain why this string has four UTF-16 code units, three Unicode scalar values, and two user-perceived characters. Why would taking `text[0]` fail to extract the first complete displayed character, and which .NET API works at the user-perceived-character boundary?

rubric.point: Explains that the rocket uses two UTF-16 code units, while `n` and the combining tilde use one each, giving `Length == 4`.
Explains that the rocket is one Unicode scalar value, with `n` and the combining tilde contributing one each, giving three scalar values.
Explains that `n` plus the combining tilde forms one grapheme, so the string contains two user-perceived characters.
Explains that `text[0]` returns only one surrogate code unit and identifies `StringInfo` text-element APIs as suitable for grapheme boundaries.

questions.model:
The rocket is outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, so UTF-16 represents it with a surrogate pair: two code units. `n` and the combining tilde each use one more code unit, making `text.Length` equal to 4.

The surrogate pair represents one Unicode scalar value. Together with `n` and the combining tilde, that gives three scalar values; `EnumerateRunes()` operates at this boundary.

The combining tilde joins the preceding `n` into one grapheme. The rocket is another grapheme, giving two user-perceived characters.

`text[0]` returns a single `char`, which is only the first half of the rocket's surrogate pair. `StringInfo` text-element APIs operate on grapheme clusters and can extract complete user-perceived characters.
